subject: Biology
title: Why We Sleep
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Why We Sleep.

hook.text: Every animal with a brain sleeps. Going without it can kill you faster than starvation.

buildup.text: During sleep, the brain clears toxic waste, consolidates memories, and repairs itself.

discovery.text: The glymphatic system flushes out harmful proteins like beta-amyloid, linked to Alzheimer's.

twist.text: Rats deprived of sleep die within two weeks—before rats deprived of food.

climax.text: Chronic sleep loss raises the risk of heart disease, diabetes, depression, and dementia.

punchline.text: Sleep isn't wasted time. It's survival time.

quiz.question: What does the glymphatic system do during sleep?
options: Flushes toxic waste from the brain

details.summary: Sleep is essential for memory consolidation, brain waste clearance, immune function, emotional regulation, and cellular repair. The glymphatic system clears toxic waste products including amyloid-beta during sleep, making it literally a brain-cleaning process.
details.whyItMatters: Sleep deprivation impairs cognition, weakens immunity, increases disease risk, and may accelerate neurodegeneration. Understanding why sleep is biologically essential has transformed it from an optional luxury into a recognized health priority.
takeaways: The glymphatic system clears toxic brain waste during sleep
Sleep deprivation impairs memory, judgment, and immune function
Chronic poor sleep increases risk of Alzheimer's and cardiovascular disease

faq.question: What is the glymphatic system?
faq.answer: The glymphatic system is a brain waste clearance network that becomes most active during deep sleep. Cerebrospinal fluid flows through brain tissue, flushing out metabolic waste including amyloid-beta protein linked to Alzheimer's disease.

faq.question: How much sleep do adults actually need?
faq.answer: Research consistently shows that 7 to 9 hours provides optimal cognitive and physical function for most adults. People who claim to thrive on less typically show measurable impairments in testing. True short sleepers who need less than 6 hours are extremely rare.
